**Analysis of the test image:**

**Affected plant part:** Leaf of a wheat/small grain plant (narrow monocot blade)

**Key visual features:**
- A distinct pale yellow to tan longitudinal streak running from near the leaf tip downward, parallel to the leaf veins
- The streak occupies a portion of the leaf width (roughly central/one side), with green tissue remaining on either side and toward the leaf base
- The discoloration is linear and vein-parallel — not spotty, pustular, or mosaic
- The lower portion of the leaf retains normal green color, with a gradual green-to-yellow transition
- No visible orange/yellow powdery pustules (rules out stripe rust or leaf rust)
- No discrete oval or diamond-shaped tan lesions (rules out tan spot or septoria blotch)

**Reasoning:**
The hallmark feature here is a single, continuous pale yellow/tan stripe running parallel to the leaf veins from tip toward base. This pattern is the classic presentation of **Cephalosporium Stripe**, caused by the soilborne fungus *Cephalosporium gramineum*, which colonizes the vascular tissue and produces one or more distinct pale-yellow to white stripes aligned with the veins. The remaining green tissue on either side of the streak and the tip-to-base gradient are consistent with vascular colonization progressing from root uptake upward. Bacterial streak and bacterial leaf streak would typically show more water-soaked margins and multiple lesions; BYDV would cause broader leaf yellowing with reddish tints; stripe rust would have pustule rows.
